qt: to the Commission Marcin Sypniewski (ESN) Subject:

According to HELCOM, approximately 40 000 tonnes of chemical munitions containing roughly 15 000 tonnes of chemical warfare agents were dumped in the Baltic Sea following the Second World War. Significant quantities of conventional munitions also lie on the seabed. The corrosion of these materials poses a threat to the marine environment, the fishing industry and underwater infrastructure. Despite many years of research and EU-funded projects, practical operations to physically remove these hazards remain limited. As part of its 2025 European Ocean Pact, the Commission announced the development of a comprehensive strategy to clear the dumped munitions. In light of this: 1.

Has the Commission drawn up cost estimates for the safe removal or neutralisation of dumped munitions from the Baltic Sea that take into account the areas of greatest environmental risk, and if not, when does it plan to do so?

Does the Commission intend to secure dedicated funding within the next EU multiannual financial framework for the actual removal and neutralisation of the munitions, and to set out a timetable and measurable targets for reducing the environmental hazards in question?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.11.2026) The Commission recognises the environmental, safety and economic risks associated with conventional and chemical munitions dumped in European seas, particularly in the Baltic Sea. Over the years, the EU has supported several projects aimed at improving knowledge, mapping and risk assessment, as well as developing technologies and approaches for the safe remediation of underwater unexploded ordnance, including chemical munitions. The costs of remediation are very difficult to assess at this stage, as they depend on a range of factors, including the type, location and condition of the munitions, the environmental and safety risks involved, and the remediation methods applied. In the context of the ongoing preparations of the Strategy for the safe remediation of unexploded ordnance in European seas, risk assessment and prioritisation, available remediation technologies and related financing needs are being assessed, with particular attention to areas where intervention may be most needed. The Commission continues to support relevant activities through existing EU funding instruments, including the European Maritime, Fisheries, and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF)1, Horizon Europe2, the European Regional Development Fund3 and others4. In the context of the preparation of the above-mentioned Strategy, consideration will also be given to possible financing options, as well as appropriate objectives and mechanisms to monitor progress. Considerations concerning funding under the next Multiannual Financial Framework will take into account relevant EU programs and their respective priorities, as well as possible complementarities with national funding.
